learn.title: Split, solve, combine
learn.body: Divide and conquer is a recursion pattern. Divide the problem into smaller pieces, conquer each piece by solving it with the same method, then combine the answers. Merge sort and binary search follow it.

learn.title: Summing an array by halves
learn.body: The base case is a single item. Otherwise add the sums of the two halves.

learn.title: Binary search, recursively
learn.body: It discards one half and searches the other. The base case is an empty range, which returns -1.

learn.title: Why it can be fast
learn.body: Each call halves the range, so there are about $\log n$ levels. In binary search each level does one comparison, giving $O(\log n)$. In merge sort each level merges all n items, giving $O(n \log n)$. The cost depends on the work per level.

learn.title: rsum on {3, 1, 4, 1}
steps: `rsum(a, 0, 3)` splits at `mid` 1 into indexes 0 to 1 and 2 to 3
Each half splits again until single items, which are the base case

learn.body: Merge sort is the full picture: split, recursively sort both halves, then merge, using the merge function from the Sorting unit.

questions.prompt: What are the three steps of divide and conquer?
questions.explanation: Split the problem, solve the parts, then join the answers.

questions.prompt: What is the base case of `rsum`?
questions.explanation: A range with one item has the sum equal to that item.

questions.prompt: `rbin` searches `{1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13}` for 11. What index does it return?
questions.explanation: 11 is at index 5. The first middle is 7, so it recurses on the right half.
4 is not in the array, so the range eventually becomes empty and the base case returns -1.

questions.prompt: Recursive binary search has about \_\_ levels of calls for n items.
Why does merge sort cost $O(n \log n)$?
choices: About log n levels, each doing n work
n levels doing log n work
questions.explanation: Halving gives log n levels, and each level merges all n items.
